The map's name, in its 1815 snapshot, for the Sokoto Caliphate, the state that Fulani Muslim scholars and herders built across what is now northern Nigeria. In 1815 it was barely ten years old.

In 1804 the preacher Usman dan Fodio declared a jihad against the Hausa kings, whom he accused of unjust taxes and of enslaving Muslims. By 1808 his followers held the Hausa cities, and they pressed on toward Bornu in the east and into Nupe and Yoruba land in the south.

Usman soon withdrew to teaching and writing. His son Muhammad Bello ruled the eastern half from Sokoto, and his brother Abdullahi the western half from Gwandu, with an emir over each province. His daughter Nana Asma'u became a famous poet and teacher of women. The British conquered the caliphate in 1903.
